reference.title: British and European Butterflies and Moths (Macrolepidoptera), plate VIII figure 3

doc: *Aglais io*, upperside, wings spread — the peacock butterfly.
Traced from figure 3 of plate VIII of W. E. Kirby's *British and European
Butterflies and Moths*, captioned under the old name *Vanessa io*, with the
larva beside it as 3a. `references/aglais-io.jpg` is the plate and
`references/SOURCES.md` has the provenance.
The figure is drawn at an angle across the sheet rather than square to it,
which is normal for a book that fits six butterflies on a page and is why
nothing here is a coordinate lifted off the scan. What was taken is the
wing shape, the eyespot positions and the proportions; the plate is drawn
square, because a plate that inherited the page's layout would be a drawing
of a book.
## What the drawing has to get right
The **eyespots**, and there is nothing else close. Four of them, one to a
wing, and they are why the animal is called a peacock: a dark outer ring, a
paler inner ring, and a bright off-centre pupil that reads as a highlight.
Each is drawn as those three parts rather than as one shape, because a
single ellipse is a spot and the ringing is the whole effect. `markings:
'eyespots'` is the only record in the archive that says so, and this is the
drawing of that word.
Then the **forewing apex**, which on a peacock is squared off and very
slightly hooked, with a shallow scoop out of the outer margin below it. A
rounded apex turns it into a tortoiseshell — which is figure 2 on the same
plate, and the animal it is most often confused with.
The **dark border** round both wings, with the paler band just inside it, is
drawn as two strips: the margin traced, and a depth inwards. Bands that keep
their width round a curve, rather than wedges.
## No legs
A nymphalid with its wings spread shows none from above, and
`REQUIRED_PARTS.lepidoptera` does not ask for them. This family has only
four walking legs anyway — the forelegs are reduced to brushes held against
the thorax — and none of that is visible in dorsal view.
## Plate space
y = 0 at the front of the head, y = 1000 at the tip of the abdomen. The
forewing apex reaches x = 1420 and y = -336; the hindwing reaches y = 1010.
The body is a tenth of the span, which is what a nymphalid is.

note: The hind wing first, so the forewing overlaps it at the base, which is
the way round a spread butterfly is put together.
The venation, as nine strokes fanning from the wing base to the margin.
Kirby's lithograph carries the veins as breaks in the colour rather than
as lines; drawn as lines here, because an engraving has no other way to
say a wing is a membrane on a frame.
The pale band and the dark border, as two strips on one traced margin.
The pale one is drawn first and reaches seventy-four units in from the edge;
the border is drawn over it and reaches fifty-six. What shows of the
wider strip is the band, which is how an engraver would get it and
means one measured edge rather than two — the second of which would be
the first offset by hand, and wrong by a few units all the way round.
The hindwing eyespot: three parts, drawn outward in. A dark outer ring, a
paler inner ring, and an off-centre pupil in bare paper.
One shape would be a spot. What makes an eyespot is that it is ringed and
that the highlight is not in the middle of it, which is the trick every
animal with eyespots is playing and the reason they work at all.
The fore wing. The apex is squared off and faintly hooked and the outer
margin is scooped just below it — a rounded apex would make this a small
tortoiseshell, which is figure 2 on the same plate.
The pale band and the dark border, as two strips on one traced margin.
The pale one is drawn first and reaches seventy-four units in from the edge;
the border is drawn over it and reaches fifty-six. What shows of the
wider strip is the band, which is how an engraver would get it and
means one measured edge rather than two — the second of which would be
the first offset by hand, and wrong by a few units all the way round.
The abdomen. Stout for a butterfly and short — a peacock overwinters as
an adult and carries the fat to do it.
The thorax, furred, and drawn once on the axis. The three hatching
strokes are the fur; a filled shape would be a beetle's pronotum.
A clubbed antenna, which is what puts this animal with the butterflies
rather than the moths — and the character that separates it from the
death's-head hawkmoth two accessions later, whose antennae taper to a
point. Two strokes for the shaft and a filled club at the end.
